newsitem.title: UK: UK domestic orders up, exports tumble - CBI.
newsitem.headline: UK domestic orders up, exports tumble - CBI.

text.p: Demand for manufacturing goods in the British domestic market rose at its fastest rate in two yaers over the four months to April, but export orders fell back, the Confederation of British Industry said on Wednesday.

The CBI's quarterly industrial trends survey showed 31 percent of firms reported rising domestic orders volumes in the last four months while 23 percent said it was down -- leaving a positive balance of eight percent.
"This rate of growtt, although below expectations, was the highest in two years," the CBI said.
"By contrast, the balance of seven percent of firms reporting a fall in export orders, represents the sharpest fall since late 1993," it said.
Both domestic and, to a lesser extent export orders, are predicted to improve in the next four months.
"These results show that growth has been continuing over the past few months, albeit in moderate fashion," Andrew Buxton, chairman of the CBI's economic affairs committee said.
"The overall manufacturing performance masked a divergent trend in demand. Domestic orders are doing well while demand from overseas is suffering from the continued strength of sterling," he said.
The high level of sterling had also resulted in a reported fall in export prices and a sharp fall in exporters' optimism.

"Although a strong upswing is now expected in both demand and output, the pace of this growth could well be overstated given the present state of export orders, and manufacturers' persistent over-optimism over the past two years," Buxton said.
"More positively, it seems very likely to be growth associated with weak price pressures," he said.
Looking ahead, unit costs are set to fall at the sharpest rate on record, the CBI said, referring to a balance of minus 10 on average unit costs over the next four months.
Prices are now a larger constraint for winning export orders with 74 percent of firms citing them as an obstacle, the highest level reported since July 1981.
Export optimism for the year ahead -- a balance of minus 16 percent -- has fallen at the sharpest rate for six years.
